payload.rationale: To determine if 2026 will be the hottest year on record (above 2025 and >1.28°C on the NASA GISS index), we must consider the long-term warming trend and the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle. Global temperatures have a strong upward trajectory, making new records frequent. However, 2023 and 2024 featured a strong El Niño, which typically spikes global temperatures. By 2026, the ENSO cycle may have transitioned to a La Niña or neutral phase, which generally depresses global average temperatures relative to the trend line. Without real-time data for 2025 and the first eight months of 2026, we must rely on historical patterns where record-breaking years often cluster around El Niño events rather than occurring consecutively every year. Strongest reason the estimate could be too high: 2026 might be a strong La Niña year, significantly cooling the global average and making a new record highly unlikely. Strongest reason the estimate could be too low: The underlying anthropogenic warming trend could be accelerating faster than anticipated, or a new El Niño could develop by late 2026, pushing temperatures above the 1.28°C threshold and past 2025 regardless of previous cycles.
limitations: No current data for 2024, 2025, or 2026 year-to-date temperatures or ENSO forecasts are available.
